newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus unhappy with Europe statement on joining.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus unhappy with Europe statement on joining.

text.p: Cyprus said on Tuesday it was unhappy with a push by European states to include a contentious phrase in a statement on the island's talks to join the European Union.
The reference to the involvement of "all Cypriots" in the entry negotiations of the divided island was attacked by Cypriot government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides.
The Greek Cypriot-led administration, internationally recognised as the island's only government and the EU's "sole interlocutor", is to start accession talks with the bloc next year.
But Greece and the Greek Cypriots fear "all Cypriots" could include Turkish Cypriots whose breakaway state in the north is recognised only by Ankara.

"If one wanted to exploit this phraseology...it would complicate the issue of Cyprus's entry in a manner which would not facilitate the course of Cyprus for accession, or the solution of the Cyprus problem," Cassoulides said.
Greece, Cyprus's closest ally, is opposing a push by the other 14 members away from a policy that Cyprus's membership could be limited to its southern Greek Cypriot part.
Local newspapers and the semi-official media said the contentious wording was backed by Britain, Germany and France.
"The intentions of the three countries as they have been expressed are not satisfactory...they are not positive enough," said Cassoulides.

Diplomats in Europe have said the stance by Greece's 14 EU partners was to pressure Athens to negotiate a settlement to the divided island. Turkey invaded the northern third in 1974 after a brief Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia that was backed by Athens.

"Greece correctly did not accept the proposed phraseology because such phraseology was open to multiple interpretations," said the government official, referring to the EU decision to start accession negotiations.

United Nations-led attempts to reunite the island under a federal umbrella have had little progress while tension between Greek and Turkish Cypriots has risen after killings at the ceasefire line and a decision by Greek Cypriots to purchase anti-aircraft missiles from Russia.
That deal prompted threats from Turkey of a military strike to block deployment of the missiles, due in 16 months. Ankara has some 30,000 troops in northern Cyprus.
